content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that individuals engage in 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. However, the majority of people fail to meet this guideline. Workplaces provide a unique opportunity to influence behavior and promote physical activity, as well as other aspects of a healthy lifestyle. Pedometers, which are relatively inexpensive devices, have traditionally been used to encourage physical activity by providing feedback on daily step counts. However, pedometers are increasingly being replaced by more advanced technologies, such as accelerometers and smartphone applications. This review represents the final update on the effectiveness of workplace pedometer interventions. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of workplace pedometer interventions in increasing physical activity and improving long-term health outcomes. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted. The search covered records from their inception to December 2016, with an additional update in May 2019. However, the results from the 2019 update have not yet been incorporated into the analysis. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving employed adults and including a pedometer component were selected for inclusion. Studies were excluded if they involved athletes, used accelerometers instead of pedometers, or did not measure physical activity as an outcome. A total of 14 studies, involving 4,762 participants, were included in the review. These studies were conducted in various high-income countries and included diverse workplace settings, ranging from office environments to more physically demanding workplaces. Participants included both healthy individuals and those at risk of chronic diseases, such as those with sedentary lifestyles or overweight individuals. The average age of participants was 41 years. All studies employed multi-component health promotion interventions, with 11 studies using minimal intervention controls and four studies comparing pedometer interventions to alternative physical activity interventions. The duration of the interventions ranged from one week to two years, with follow-up periods lasting between three and ten months after the interventions ended. The overall quality of the evidence was low, with most studies rated as having an unclear or high risk of bias. Only one study was rated as having a low risk of bias. Common methodological concerns included the lack of blinding and high rates of participant attrition. When comparing pedometer interventions to minimal interventions at follow-up points at least one month after the intervention, the evidence suggested that pedometers may have no significant effect on physical activity levels. However, the certainty of this evidence was very low, and the results were highly heterogeneous, precluding meta-analysis. Similarly, pedometer interventions may have uncertain effects on sedentary behavior and quality of life (mental health component), based on very low-certainty evidence from a single study. Pedometer interventions may lead to a slight reduction in anthropometric measures, such as body mass index (BMI), with a mean difference of -0.64 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.45 to 0.18) based on low-certainty evidence from three studies. However, pedometer interventions likely have little to no effect on blood pressure, with a mean difference in systolic blood pressure of -0.08 mmHg (95% CI: -3.26 to 3.11) based on moderate-certainty evidence from two studies. Additionally, pedometer interventions may reduce adverse events, such as injuries, with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.50 (95% CI: 0.30 to 0.84) based on low-certainty evidence. No studies compared biochemical measures or disease risk scores at follow-up between pedometer interventions and minimal interventions. When comparing pedometer interventions to alternative physical activity interventions, the evidence suggested that pedometers may have an effect on physical activity levels, but the certainty of this evidence was very low. Other outcomes, such as sedentary behavior, anthropometric measures (e.g., BMI or waist circumference), blood pressure, biochemical markers (e.g., LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, or triglycerides), disease risk scores, quality of life, and adverse effects, were not compared between pedometer interventions and alternative physical activity interventions. Some positive effects were observed immediately after the completion of intervention periods, but these effects were inconsistent, and the overall certainty of the evidence was insufficient to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of workplace pedometer interventions. In conclusion, while exercise interventions in general can have positive effects on employee physical activity and health, the current evidence does not support the notion that pedometer-based interventions are more effective than other options. It is important to note that advances in technology, particularly the widespread availability of accelerometers in commercial products and smartphones, have rendered pedometers somewhat obsolete. Future studies should focus on identifying the effective components of multi-component interventions and consider strategies to sustain behavioral changes and intervention effects over the long term. Additionally, more consistent measures of physical activity and health outcomes are needed to improve the quality of evidence in this field. Decision-makers should exercise caution when allocating resources to large-scale pedometer-based programs, as the benefits may not be sustained over time.
